title: The First Assessment of PhiSat-2 Imagery for Monocular Building Height Estimation
summary: PhiSat-2 provides multispectral observations at a 4.75m spatial resolution across geographically diverse scenes, offering a new source of remote sensing imagery for monocular building-height estimation. To comprehensively assess its utility, this study introduces the PhiSat-2--Height Dataset (PHDataset) and the Two-Stream Ordinal Network (TSONet). PHDataset integrates global PhiSat-2 imagery with open building-height references and contains 9475 co-registered patch pairs from 26 cities worldwide. In TSONet, multiscale decoupled height representation (MDHR) separates adaptive bin generation from spatial assignment, while footprint-conditioned height reconstruction (FCHR) incorporates footprint guidance at feature and reconstruction levels. Under city-disjoint evaluation, TSONet reduces building RMSE and MAE by 3.64% and 4.49%, respectively, relative to the most accurate comparison method originally designed for building-height estimation, while maintaining similar height-derived footprint IoU. Ablations support the combined design for height accuracy and footprint consistency. PhiSat-2 reduces building RMSE by 3.73% and 6.05% relative to the evaluated Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8 configurations, respectively, with all seven bands providing the lowest building-height errors among its tested band subsets. LiDAR-based testing supports PHDataset-style supervision in a held-out city, while selected patch comparisons show finer urban height patterns than coarser global products. These findings highlight the value of PhiSat-2 spatial-spectral information for urban building height mapping, with PHDataset and TSONet providing a foundation for further development.

title: F2F-AP: Flow-to-Future Asynchronous Policy for Real-time Dynamic Manipulation
summary: Asynchronous inference has emerged as a prevalent paradigm in robotic manipulation, achieving significant progress in ensuring trajectory smoothness and efficiency. However, a systemic challenge remains unresolved, as inherent latency causes generated actions to inevitably lag behind the real-time environment. This issue is particularly exacerbated in dynamic scenarios, where such temporal misalignment severely compromises the policy's ability to interpret and react to rapidly evolving surroundings. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that leverages predicted object flow to synthesize future observations, incorporating a flow-based contrastive learning objective to align the visual feature representations of predicted observations with ground-truth future states. Empowered by this anticipated visual context, our asynchronous policy gains the capacity for proactive planning and motion, enabling it to explicitly compensate for latency and robustly execute manipulation tasks involving actively moving objects. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances responsiveness and success rates in complex dynamic manipulation tasks.

title: Towards Better Aligned LLM Judges for Radiology Report Evaluation across Modalities and Anatomies
summary: Current work on radiology report evaluation has focused primarily on LLM-based metrics for chest X-rays (CXR), leaving open whether such approaches remain robust across other modalities and anatomies, and which model and prompt configurations are best suited to serve as LLM judges. We present a comprehensive evaluation of LLM judges for radiology report evaluation across diverse model families, prompting strategies, and adaptation methods, leveraging two expert-annotated datasets that span multiple imaging modalities and anatomical regions. Specifically, we compare four existing metrics (RadFact, GREEN, FineRadScore, and CRIMSON) with our proposed metric, VERT, across open- and closed-source models of varying sizes and reasoning capabilities. Among existing metrics, GREEN proves the most robust, outperforming more recent CXR-specific approaches. VERT further improves Kendall's correlation with radiologist judgment by up to 26% over GREEN, while ensembling and lightweight fine-tuning of Qwen3-30B yield gains of up to 9.9% and 25%, respectively, of which the latter also has a latency reduction of 37.2x. A systematic error analysis further shows that, while these metrics correlate with expert ratings overall, they tend to miscount errors such as omissions. Overall, our results show that carefully selected general-purpose LLM judges provide strong radiology report evaluation across modalities, with lightweight adaptation offering complementary gains when annotated data is available.

title: Where to Steer: Input-Dependent Layer Selection for Steering Improves LLM Alignment
summary: Steering vectors have emerged as a lightweight and effective approach for aligning large language models (LLMs) at inference time, enabling modulation of model behaviors by shifting intermediate representations toward a target behavior. Many existing steering methods apply interventions at globally fixed locations in an LLM, effectively treating the optimal intervention location as input-invariant. However, representations relevant to a target behavior can be encoded at different LLM layers depending on the input. Theoretically, we show that different inputs may require steering at different layers to achieve alignment with a given behavior. Empirically, we observe that the most effective layer for steering varies substantially between inputs. Motivated by these observations, we introduce \textit{Where to Steer} (W2S), a general framework that adaptively selects intervention layers conditioned on the inputs by learning a mapping from input representations to steering layers. Across multiple LLMs and alignment behaviors, W2S consistently outperforms fixed-layer baselines in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. Our findings suggest that input-dependent layer selection is a key design dimension complementary to methods for steering vector extraction.

title: A Gradual Probabilistic Lambda Calculus
summary:
Probabilistic programming languages extend ordinary programming languages with the ability to sample values from probability distributions. Type systems can establish invariants of such programs, for instance by assigning to a program a distribution over types that specifies the probability of each kind of outcome. However, adopting such a type discipline can be cumbersome or overly conservative.
  Gradual typing addresses this problem by supporting a smooth transition between static and dynamic checking, and has been successfully applied for languages with different constructs and type abstractions. Nevertheless, its benefits have never been explored in the context of probabilistic languages.
  In this work, we present and formalize GLANG, a gradual source probabilistic lambda calculus. GLANG includes a binary probabilistic choice operator and allows programmers to gradually introduce/remove static type---and probability---annotations. The static semantics of GLANG heavily relies on the notion of probabilistic couplings, as required for defining several relations, such as consistency, precision, and consistent transitivity. The dynamic semantics of GLANG is given via elaboration to the target language TLANG, which features a distribution-based semantics interpreting programs as probability distributions over final values. Regarding the language metatheory, we establish that TLANG---and therefore also GLANG---is type safe and satisfies two of the so-called refined criteria for gradual languages, namely, that it is a conservative extension of a fully static variant and that it satisfies (a restricted form of) the gradual guarantee, behaving smoothly with respect to type precision. The metatheory is mechanized in the Lean 4 proof assistant.

title: ORACLE-SWE: Quantifying the Contribution of Critical Information Signals on SWE Agents
comments: Under peer review; 31 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables
summary: Recent advances in Language Model (LM) agents have increasingly focused on repository-level software engineering (SWE) tasks, leading to various agentic workflows, training methods and failure analysis. Interestingly, rather than directly generating or evaluating edit patches, these approaches first examine and improve intermediate information signals collected during agent exploration, including Reproduction Test, Regression Test, Edit Location, Execution Context, and API Usage. Although different studies examine different subsets of these signals, no work has systematically compared their relative effectiveness in improving final task success or measured the remaining space for improvement in each signal. To address this gap, this work quantifies the contributions of both oracle and agent-extracted signals to final task success and measures the gap between current agent-found signals and their oracle counterparts. We hope our findings could suggest future research emphasis in SWE agents. We release our source code and oracle-signal dataset as a reusable methodology to benefit future signal analysis of SWE agents.
comment: Under peer review; 31 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables

title: Wattlytics: A Web Platform for Co-Optimizing Performance, Energy, and TCO in HPC Clusters
summary: The escalating computational demands and energy footprint of GPU-accelerated computing systems complicate informed design and operational decisions. We present the first release of Wattlytics (https://wattlytics.netlify.app), an interactive, browser-based decision-support system. Unlike existing procurement-oriented calculators, Wattlytics uniquely integrates benchmark-driven GPU performance scaling, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)-aware piecewise power modeling, and multi-year total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis within a single interactive environment. Users can configure heterogeneous systems across contemporary GPU architectures (GH200, H100, L40S, L40, A40, A100, and L4), select representative scientific workloads (e.g., GROMACS, AMBER), and explore deployment scenarios under constraints such as energy prices, system lifetime, and frequency scaling. Wattlytics computes multidimensional decision metrics (TCO breakdown, work-per-TCO, power-per-TCO, and work-per-watt-per-TCO) and supports design-space exploration, what-if scenarios, sensitivity metrics (elasticity, Sobol indices, Monte Carlo) and collaborative features to guide realistic cluster design and procurement under uncertainty. We validate the fitted power and performance models and compare four deployment modes: fixed budget, fixed GPU count, fixed performance, and fixed power. Our case studies show that, under budget or energy constraints, optimally deployed energy-efficient GPUs can outperform higher-performance alternatives in overall cost-effectiveness. Wattlytics helps users explore the design parameter space and distinguish between cost- and risk-driving factors, turning HPC design into a well-informed and explainable decision-making process.

title: Sim-to-Real Transfer for Muscle-Actuated Robots via Generalized Actuator Networks
summary: Tendon drives paired with soft muscle actuation enable faster and safer robots while potentially accelerating skill acquisition. Still, these systems are rarely used in practice due to inherent nonlinearities, friction, and hysteresis, which complicate modeling and control. So far, these challenges have hindered policy transfer from simulation to real systems. To bridge this gap, we propose a sim-to-real pipeline that learns a neural network model of this complex actuation and leverages established rigid body simulation for the arm dynamics and interactions with the environment. Our method, called Generalized Actuator Network (GenAN), enables actuation model identification across a wide range of robots by learning directly from joint position trajectories rather than requiring torque sensors. Using GenAN on PAMY2, a tendon-driven robot powered by pneumatic artificial muscles, we successfully deploy dynamic but precise goal-reaching, ball-in-a-cup, and table tennis policies, trained entirely in simulation. To the best of our knowledge, this result constitutes the first successful sim-to-real transfer for a four-degrees-of-freedom muscle-actuated robot arm.

title: PhyMix: Towards Physically Consistent Single-Image 3D Indoor Scene Generation with Implicit--Explicit Optimization
summary: Existing methods for single-image 3D indoor scene generation often produce visually plausible results that violate real-world physical constraints, limiting their reliability in robotics, embodied AI, and virtual environment design. To bridge this gap, we introduce a Physics Evaluator that assesses four aspects (geometric priors, contact, stability, and deployability) through nine sub-constraints, establishing a benchmark for evaluating physical consistency. Our analysis reveals that even state-of-the-art methods produce scenes with substantial physical inconsistencies despite their visual plausibility. To address these limitations, we propose a framework that incorporates feedback from the Physics Evaluator into both training and inference to improve the physical plausibility of generated scenes. Specifically, PhyMix comprises two components: (i) implicit alignment via Scene-GRPO, a critic-free group-relative preference optimization strategy that uses physical evaluations to guide the generator toward physically plausible layouts, and (ii) explicit refinement via verifier-guided agentic repair, which translates evaluator diagnostics into executable scene-editing skills to correct residual violations at inference time. PhyMix unifies physical evaluation, preference-based alignment, and agentic inference-time correction to improve physical plausibility while retaining the observed scene content. Experiments show improvements in reconstruction quality and physical plausibility, while qualitative examples on stylized and real-world images illustrate the applicability of the framework beyond synthetic inputs.

title: Naka-GS: Naka-Guided Chroma Correction and Point-Prior Compaction for Low-Light 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Low-light inputs obscure scene content, distort color, and corrupt geometric priors, substantially degrading 3D Gaussian Splatting. Although image enhancement can recover visibility, it often introduces chromatic deviations and fine-scale artifacts that propagate through multi-view reconstruction. Moreover, dense point priors can further amplify these errors and increase optimization cost. To address the coupled challenges, we present Naka-GS, a low-light 3DGS framework that jointly improves observations and Gaussian initialization while retaining the standard 3DGS renderer and training objective. Our Naka-Guided Chroma Correction treats a fixed bionic response as a photometric anchor and learns bounded, frequency-decoupled luminance and chromatic corrections, preserving fine structures while suppressing residual color and boundary artifacts. The corrected views are reconstructed into dense scene priors, which a lightweight, non-learned Point-Prior Compaction Module refines through voxel pooling and distance-adaptive progressive pruning. On eight scene-disjoint RealX3D scenes, Naka-GS achieves 20.735~dB PSNR, 0.7408 SSIM, and 0.3340 LPIPS. PPM reduces initialization from 1.00M to 59.52K points and shortens average 3DGS optimization time by 37.7%.The code is available at https://github.com/RunyuZhu/Naka-GS

title: MIXAR: Scaling Autoregressive Pixel-based Language Models to Multiple Languages and Scripts
summary: Pixel-based language models are gaining momentum as alternatives to traditional token-based approaches, promising to circumvent tokenization challenges; however, existing models remain English-centric and are hard to train as generators. This paper introduces MIXAR, the first generative multilingual pixel-based language model, pretrained on eight high-resource languages spanning Latin and CJK scripts and scaled up to 0.5B parameters. Although pretrained on high-resource languages only, MIXAR generalizes to unseen low-resource languages better than a tokenizer-based model pretrained on the same corpus, with its largest gains on the scripts most distant from the pretraining mix, taking a step toward more equitable language technology. To make free generation work in pixel space, MIXAR replaces the notoriously unstable adversarial training stage of prior pixel-based models with a GRPO-based reinforcement-learning stage that rewards the model on its own free-running generations: it proves more stable and multiplies free-generation accuracy by up to 2.3x on multilingual benchmarks. Finally, MIXAR performs on par with comparable tokenizer-based models on discriminative benchmarks, improves consistently with scale, and withstands orthographic attacks more gracefully than tokenizer-based models. Code and models are available at https://github.com/april-tools/mixar.

title: V-GIFT: Boosting Visual Instruction Tuning with Self-Supervised Guidance
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) perform well on many vision-language tasks but often struggle with vision-centric problems that require fine-grained visual perception. Recent evidence suggests that this limitation arises not from weak visual representations, but from under-utilization of visual information during instruction tuning, where many tasks can be partially solved using language priors alone. We propose a simple and lightweight approach that augments visual instruction tuning with a small number of visually grounded self-supervised tasks expressed as natural language instructions. By reformulating classical self-supervised pretext tasks, such as rotation prediction, color matching, and cross-view correspondence, as image-instruction-response triplets, we introduce supervision that cannot be solved without relying on visual evidence. Our approach requires no human annotations, no architectural modifications, and no additional training stages. Across multiple models, training regimes, and benchmarks, injecting only a small fraction (3-10%) of such visually grounded instructions consistently improves performance on vision-centric evaluations. Our findings highlight instruction tuning with visually grounded SSL tasks as a powerful lever for improving visual perception in MLLMs through simple adjustments to the training data distribution. Code available at: https://github.com/sirkosophia/V-GIFT

title: TensorDex: A Compact, Tensor-Centric Storage System for Modern AI Models
comments: 12 pages, 6 figures. Systems paper on AI model storage
summary:
Modern model hubs store hundreds of petabytes of large language models (LLMs), with fine-tuned variants dominating the storage footprint. These variants contain substantial cross-model redundancy that delta compression can exploit by storing only the difference between a target and a reference model. However, compression effectiveness depends critically on choosing a similar reference. At model-hub scale, this is challenging because model lineage metadata is often missing or unreliable, and different tensors within the same model may be most similar to tensors from different models. Consequently, model-level pairing leaves substantial redundancy unexploited.
  We present TensorDex, a lossless, tensor-centric storage system that performs delta compression at tensor granularity. TensorDex decomposes models into tensors, uses compact bit-level fingerprints to predict tensor-pair compressibility, and incrementally organizes tensors into multi-center clusters to select effective bases as new models arrive. Evaluated on 2,890 randomly sampled Hugging Face models, TensorDex reduces storage footprint by 70.5%, 37% lower than the state-of-the-art design. It achieves 22.9 GB/s compression and 28.4 GB/s decompression throughput, 3.86x and 1.49x faster than the next-best system, respectively.
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures. Systems paper on AI model storage

title: Language models recognize dropout and Gaussian noise applied to their activations
summary: We provide evidence that language models can detect, localize and, to a degree, verbalize the difference between a-semantic perturbations applied to their activations. More precisely, we either (a) apply dropout or (b) add Gaussian noise to them, at a target sentence. We then ask a multiple-choice question such as "Which of the previous sentences was perturbed?" or "Which perturbation was applied?". We test eight models from the Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Olmo, Qwen and Seed families, with sizes between 8B and 36B, all of which can easily detect and localize the perturbations, often with perfect accuracy. To investigate the mechanisms, we find that Olmo models develop this capacity during pre-training, and we rule out the hypothesis that perturbed sentences simply have lower log-likelihood. Notably, the zero-shot accuracy of Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B in identifying which perturbation was applied correlates with the perturbation strength. While this task proves hard for the remaining models, most of them can learn, when taught in context, to distinguish between dropout and Gaussian noise. Interestingly, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B learn worse when supervised with wrong labels, again suggesting a prior towards the correct ones. Because dropout is used as a training-regularization technique, while Gaussian noise is sometimes added during inference, we discuss the possibility of a data-agnostic "training awareness" signal and the implications for AI safety.

title: Isolating Recurring Backend-Dependent Abnormal Patterns on NISQ Quantum Devices
summary:
Quantum hardware remains highly susceptible to noise, making compilation a critical step for obtaining reliable execution on existing devices. Today's quantum compilers approximate hardware noise using calibration-derived costs over gates, qubits, and coupling edges, and use the costs to guide qubit mapping, routing, and scheduling. However, this abstraction is incomplete: semantically equivalent circuits with identical compiler-predicted hardware noise can still behave very differently on real devices. Execution context can contribute to this gap: short ordered gate sequences on specific qubit neighborhoods can be associated with hardware-model mismatch. Identifying these backend-dependent abnormal patterns can guide gate-ordering rewrites in the circuit family and layout where they were observed.
  To find these patterns, we propose QRisk, a framework that isolates recurring abnormal gate sequences from quantum hardware executions. QRisk starts from a circuit whose hardware output is much worse than predicted by the calibration-based noise model. It then reduces the circuit at the segment level, identifying groups of segments whose removal lowers the discrepancy ratio or whose retention within the tested circuit context preserves an elevated ratio. The resulting circuit fragments are treated as candidate abnormal patterns.
  On three IBM Heron r2 backends (quantum devices) across 30 qubit layouts, QRisk finds 25 recurring abnormal gate patterns. Reordering commuting gates to break the two highest-recurrence patterns in their Grover discovery circuits reduces mean hardware-model mismatch by 24% on ibm_fez and 45% on ibm_marrakesh.

title: EmbodiedMidtrain: Bridging the Gap between Vision-Language Models and Vision-Language-Action Models via Mid-training
summary: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) inherit their visual and linguistic capabilities from Vision-Language Models (VLMs), yet most VLAs are built from off-the-shelf VLMs that are not adapted to the embodied domain, limiting their downstream performance. In this work, we propose EmbodiedMidtrain to bridge the gap between VLMs and VLAs. We first characterize the data distribution gap between them, showing that VLA data occupy compact regions that are largely separated from the broader VLM distribution, while the degree of alignment varies substantially both across and within VLM data sources. Then, we build a mid-training data engine that leverages a lightweight learnable proximity estimator to select the most VLA-aligned candidates from a large VLM pool, and produce EmbodiedMidtrain-1M, a VLM dataset that we further use to mid-train the VLM before downstream VLA fine-tuning. Experiments on both simulated robot manipulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show consistent VLA performance gains over off-the-shelf checkpoints across VLM backbones and VLA action heads. These gains extend to downstream tasks not used to guide data selection. Further analysis reveals that mid-training provides a stronger initialization for VLA fine-tuning, with gains emerging from the earliest steps and widening throughout training. Moreover, the data engine captures both dataset-level and sample-level alignment signals, favoring spatial reasoning over text-centric tasks while preserving the diversity of the VLM data. We will release all code, data and models for future research.

title: Graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equations for Power System Identification with Transfer Learning Applications
summary: With the shift towards decentralized energy generation, the increasing complexity of power systems renders physics-based modeling challenging. At the same time the growing amount of available measurement data opens the door for obtaining data-driven models. A modern method to do so are neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs), offering a framework for continuous-time system identification. Recent extensions, so called graph NODEs impose a structural inductive bias that has the potential to improve generalization of the learned representations. In this work, we employ and extend them to develop message-passing graph NODEs (MPG-NODEs) for identification of coupled systems with heterogeneous node dynamics and heterogeneous edge couplings. This includes state-of-the-art machine learning architectures to infer latent representations of unmeasured states, local node and edge embeddings to account for heterogeneity as well as an autoregressive scheme to allow for piecewise constant control inputs. We apply MPG-NODEs to identify voltage and frequency dynamics of power systems and compare them to a monolithic NODE under identical measurement assumptions. Our case study indicates that while achieving similar performance, our proposed MPG-NODEs are more flexible with transfer learning options that allow to add or remove edges and nodes with little retraining.

title: What Makes Good Instruction-Tuning Data? An In-Context Learning Perspective
summary: Instruction-tuning datasets often contain substantial redundancy and low-quality samples, necessitating effective data selection methods. We propose an instruction data selection framework based on weighted in-context influence (wICI), which measures how effectively each candidate example reduces instruction-following difficulty for semantically related peers. Through systematic experiments, we address three key questions: what constitutes effective instruction tuning data from an in-context perspective, whether sample difficulty correlates with in-context influence, and how in-context influence translates to instruction tuning effectiveness. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing baselines under constrained data budgets, while empirically showing that sample difficulty negatively correlates with in-context influence.

title: Performance Analysis of Pinching Antenna Systems Enabled NOMA Communications
comments: Update the paper content file with no highlight version from v3
summary: Pinching antenna systems (PASS) have the advantages in the perspective of flexible antenna reconfiguration, line-of-sight (LoS) creation, and scalability features. To highlight the ascendancy of PASS, we survey the integration of PASS into non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) networks. The locations of nodes are randomly distributed within a circular coverage region. The influencing factors of LoS and none-line-of-sight (NLoS) propagation links from PASS to non-orthogonal nodes are taken into consideration. To characterize performance of PASS-NOMA, we deduce the outage probability and ergodic data rates expressions of two nodes over LoS/NLoS fading channels. In light of these theoretical results, the formally unbounded diversity gains are also characterized with node n under ideal successive interference cancellation (ISIC) and node f over LoS links, when the SNR exceeds a finite threshold. The slopes of ergodic data rate for node n with ISIC equals to one and that of node f presents a zero slope. In addition, the PASS-NOMA system throughput are evaluated in different transmission modes. It is shown from the numerical results that: 1) The outage behaviors of PASS-NOMA networks under LoS/NLoS conditions outperform that of PASS aided orthogonal multiple access (OMA) networks and that of conventional antenna systems (CASS) aided OMA/NOMA networks; 2) The employment of PASS enables the larger ergodic data rates relative to PASS-OMA and CASS-OMA/NOMA networks; and 3) As the quantity of communication radius and PASS' height rises, the performance of PASS-NOMA networks are declined at a certain extent.

title: Bi-Level Optimization for Contact and Motion Planning in Rope-Assisted Legged Robots
summary: This paper presents a planning pipeline framework for locomotion in rope-assisted robots climbing vertical surfaces. The proposed framework is formulated as a bi-level optimization scheme that addresses a mixed-integer problem: selecting feasible terrain regions for landing while simultaneously optimizing the control inputs, namely rope tensions and leg forces, and landing location. The outer level of the optimization is solved using the Cross-Entropy Method, while the inner level relies on gradient-based nonlinear optimization to compute dynamically feasible motions. The approach is validated on a novel climbing robot platform, ALPINE, across a variety of challenging terrain configurations.

title: Interaction Forces and Internal Loads in Parallel Manipulators with Actuation Redundancy
comments: 30 pages, 15 figures. Accepted for publication in Mechanism and Machine Theory journal
summary: This paper discusses null-space wrench components in parallel manipulators. We examine the adaptation of the two most common characterizations of these components in grasp-like systems, namely, interaction forces and internal loads, to parallel manipulators with actuation redundancy. We identify critical oversights in the existing literature on the subject, resolve ambiguities related to the definitions of interaction forces and internal loads, and provide explicit methods for synthesizing equilibrating and manipulating joint torque vectors. A case study is also provided to justify the validity of our novel methods and correct erroneous results reported in the literature.
comment: 30 pages, 15 figures. Accepted for publication in Mechanism and Machine Theory journal

title: Mind the Gap: Structure-Aware Consistency in Preference Learning
summary: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human intent, whether through explicit reward modeling or direct methods such as DPO, fundamentally relies on minimizing a surrogate loss as a proxy for the true pairwise ranking objective. We prove that this reliance is flawed for the standard surrogate losses used: for the equicontinuous hypothesis sets characteristic of neural networks, no standard surrogate provides a meaningful consistency guarantee. Minimizing the surrogate loss to zero can leave the true ranking error arbitrarily high. To resolve this, we formulate LLM alignment within a margin-shifted ranking framework and derive $H$-consistency bounds showing that enforcing a confidence margin $γ$ is not merely beneficial but necessary for consistency. We further introduce Structure-Aware $H$-consistency and a corresponding objective (SA-DPO) that adapts the margin to the semantic distance between responses, preventing instability on near-synonymous pairs. Finally, we analyze the trade-off between the margin required for consistency and the model's finite capacity to satisfy it, revealing a strict hierarchy of surrogate losses: heavy-tailed surrogates (e.g., the Polynomial Hinge family) offer strictly superior consistency guarantees for capacity-bounded models compared to the logistic loss used in DPO. Experiments on UltraFeedback and Argilla DPO-Mix-7k confirm that SA-DPO consistently outperforms DPO and SimPO, with a 58.5% head-to-head win-rate in downstream generation quality.

title: Ideological discrepancy between Facebook pages and shared news is associated with reaction homogeneity
summary: Cross-cutting political content is often expected to mitigate polarization, yet encounters across ideological lines do not necessarily foster more constructive engagement. We analyzed 4,584 posts from 1,243 Facebook pages sharing 761 political news links in a dataset centered on Brazil's 2018 presidential election, and introduced Bias Discrepancy, which measures how far a shared link lies from the page's ideological sharing repertoire. We examined how Bias Discrepancy related to Content Reaction Positivity (how positively the same link was received in other posts), the Reaction Homogeneity Index (whether a post's own reactions were one-sided or mixed), and the toxicity of the page's accompanying text. Reaction homogeneity was lowest at both extremes of Bias Discrepancy, and posts furthest from the page's repertoire had the highest average toxicity. In a multivariable model, greater Bias Discrepancy was associated with lower reaction homogeneity, with a magnitude similar to the link's content bias and toxicity and smaller than Content Reaction Positivity. When a page shared news that departed from its repertoire, its accompanying text tended to be more toxic and its audience's reactions more mixed.

title: On the Privacy of LLMs: An Ablation Study
summary: Large language models (LLMs) face diverse privacy threats, yet existing studies typically evaluate individual attacks in isolation, offering limited guidance on which system factors drive privacy vulnerabilities. This paper presents a unified threat model and a systematic ablation study of four representative attacks: Membership Inference (MIA), Attribute Inference (AIA), Data Extraction (DEA), and Backdoor Attacks (BA). Our findings reveal attack-specific sensitivities: membership inference depends strongly on dataset characteristics and attack strategy, attribute inference is influenced by model and training characteristics, data extraction increases with model scale and training-data repetition, and backdoor attacks achieve consistently high success rates. Based on these findings, we derive practical recommendations for privacy-aware LLM deployment, including prioritizing membership leakage assessments in retrieval-augmented systems, minimizing repeated personal information in training data, monitoring attribute inference risks, and safeguarding fine-tuning pipelines against backdoors.

title: Do LLMs have core beliefs?
summary: The rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has sparked debate about whether these systems exhibit human-level cognition. In this debate, little attention has been paid to a structural component of human cognition: core beliefs, truths that provide a foundation around which we can build a worldview. These commitments usually resist debunking, as abandoning them would represent a fundamental shift in how we see reality. In this paper, we ask whether LLMs hold anything akin to core commitments. Using a probing framework we call Adversarial Dialogue Trees (ADTs) over five domains (science, history, geography, biology, and mathematics), we find that most LLMs fail to maintain a stable worldview. Though some recent models showed improved stability, they still eventually failed to maintain key commitments under conversational pressure. These results document an improvement in argumentative skills across model generations but indicate that all current models lack a key component of human-level cognition.

title: Z-Opt: A Near-Optimal Reduced-Complexity Two-Dimensional Grassmannian Constellation
summary: Grassmannian constellations achieve the capacity of noncoherent communications over Rayleigh fading channels at high SNR, yet their efficient construction remains challenging. In this paper, we present two construction methods for Grassmannian constellations on G(2,1), termed S-Opt and Z-Opt, and propose two low-complexity detectors. Both construction and detection are performed on the unit sphere, known as the Bloch sphere in quantum computing. Exploiting the proportionality between the chordal distance on the Grassmann manifold and the Euclidean distance on the Bloch sphere, we derive a theoretical upper bound on the minimum chordal distance from the Fejes-Toth bound. The S-Opt constellation is constructed from sphere-packing solutions and achieves the theoretical limit corresponding to the considered optimal Bloch-sphere packings. The S-Opt detector applies to arbitrary constellations on G(2,1) and requires a number of complex multiplications scaling linearly with the number of receive antennas and logarithmically with the constellation size, and a number of numerical comparisons scaling logarithmically with the constellation size, while achieving the same performance as the GLRT detector. Based on the insight from the S-Opt construction, we further propose the Z-Opt constellation, constructed by stacking regular polygons on the Bloch sphere, whose minimum chordal distance approaches the derived upper bound over the evaluated constellation sizes. The Z-Opt detector requires a number of complex multiplications scaling linearly with the number of receive antennas and a number of numerical comparisons scaling logarithmically with the square root of the constellation size, while achieving the same performance as the GLRT detector for the Z-Opt constellation.

title: Identifier-Free Code Embedding Models for Scalable Search
summary: Function association is a useful process for binary reverse engineers. Search tools exist to perform association at scale, but they do not utilize the full range of capabilities that AI-enabled search provides. Prior work has explored the development of embedding models for association between certain reverse engineering code representations, but that work does not cover bidirectional association between source code and decompiled, stripped code with standard preprocessing requirements. To bridge this gap, we formalize this function association problem and evaluate the extent to which embedding models can bidirectionally associate between these two representations. To improve model performance at this task, we fine-tune a Qwen3-Embedding model with contrastive learning. We find that our new model outperforms other models on all function association baselines by a substantial margin and generalizes to a constant-algorithm association task it is not explicitly trained on.

title: CRAFT: Forgetting-Aware Intervention-Based Adaptation for Continual Learning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can learn new tasks through fine-tuning, but learning tasks sequentially often leads to catastrophic forgetting of earlier ones. This paper proposes CRAFT, a continual learning framework that keeps model weights frozen and instead learns low-rank interventions on hidden representations. Similar tasks share an intervention to help knowledge transfer, with similarity judged by how each task alters the model's output distribution rather than by a learned gating network. Within a shared intervention, a Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty keeps each new task close to the intervention's existing behavior, which limits forgetting of earlier tasks, while a small, task-private intervention in the deepest layers preserves dedicated capacity that later tasks cannot overwrite. The learned interventions also make it possible to identify the task at test time, so task identity labels are not needed. Across multiple benchmarks and model scales, CRAFT improves overall performance and reduces forgetting compared with strong LoRA-based methods, while remaining robust to task ordering.

title: Towards Emotion Consistency Analysis of Large Language Models in Emotional Conversational Contexts
comments: Accepted in MultiPsyche Workshop (In Conjunction with AACL-IJCNLP 2026)
summary: In this work, we conduct an analysis to examine the consistency of Large Language Models (LLMs) with respect to their own generated responses in an emotionally-driven conversational context. Specifically, the text generated by LLM is framed as a query to the same model, and its responses are subsequently assessed. This is performed with three queries across two dimensions of extreme and moderate emotions. The three queries are, in particular, false claim queries that contain inherently wrong assumptions (false presuppositions) in increasing order of intensity. Two commercial models, Claude-3.5-haiku, GPT4o-mini, and a medium-sized model, Mistral-7B, are considered in the study. Our findings indicate that LLMs exhibit below-average performance and remain vulnerable to false beliefs embedded within queries. This susceptibility is especially pronounced for moderate emotional content. Furthermore, an extended attention-score-based analysis highlights a shift in models' priority from evaluative to generative. The results raise important considerations for LLMs' deployment in high-stakes, emotionally sensitive contexts.
comment: Accepted in MultiPsyche Workshop (In Conjunction with AACL-IJCNLP 2026)

title: Self-Programmed Execution for Language-Model Agents
comments: Camera-ready version; accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 77 pages, including appendices and checklist
summary: At the heart of a language model agent is an orchestrator program which is responsible for the state transition between consecutive turns. In existing systems, this program is implemented in the harness. This paper introduces self-programmed execution (SPE), in which the model completion is itself the orchestrator program, and the harness evaluates this program but does not impose any fixed orchestration policy. Formally, an SPE state of an agentic machine is one from which a model completion can load any successor state up to an embedding, and an instance of an SPE state is one which executes the model completion as a program. In practice, the program requires a language with unusual features, as its source code doubles as the content of the model's context window. I therefore introduce Spell, a Lisp dialect in which programs can edit and re-evaluate themselves, and effectful expressions like model invocations are structured such that re-evaluating an edited program does not replay its side effects. Experiments with existing models, not trained for SPE or Spell, show that frontier models can learn Spell in-context and accomplish challenging agentic tasks. These results demonstrate how a LM can act as an agent without any fixed orchestration policy, and they raise the question of what self-orchestration strategies might be learned by a model trained for self-programmed execution. Code is available at https://github.com/lukejoconnor/spell.
comment: Camera-ready version; accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 77 pages, including appendices and checklist

title: PathPainter: Transferring the Generalization Ability of Image Generation Models to Embodied Navigation
summary: Bird's-eye-view (BEV) images have been demonstrated to provide valuable prior information for navigation. Given the global information provided by such views, two key challenges remain: how to fully exploit this information and how to reliably use it during execution. In this paper, we propose a navigation system that uses BEV images as global priors and is designed for ground and near-ground robotic platforms. The system employs an image generation model to interpret human intent from natural language, identify the target destination, and generate traversability masks. During execution, we introduce cross-view localization to align the robot's odometry with the BEV map and mitigate long-term drift in conventional odometry. We conduct extensive benchmark experiments to evaluate the proposed method and further validate its effectiveness on both UAV and quadruped robot platforms. Using only a conventional local motion planner, the quadruped robot successfully completes a 285-meter outdoor long-range navigation task. This work demonstrates how the world-understanding capabilities of foundation models can be transferred to embodied navigation, enabling robots to benefit from the strong generalization ability of existing image generation models.

title: SimCT: Recovering Lost Supervision for Cross-Tokenizer On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a standard tool for transferring teacher behavior to a smaller student, but it implicitly assumes that teacher and student predictions are comparable token by token, an assumption that fails whenever the two models tokenize the same text differently. Under heterogeneous tokenizers, exact shared-token matching silently discards a large fraction of the teacher signal at precisely the positions where vocabularies disagree. We propose \textbf{\underline{Sim}ple \underline{C}ross-\underline{T}okenizer OPD (SimCT)}, which restores this signal by enlarging the supervision space: alongside shared tokens, SimCT compares teacher and student over short multi-token continuations that both tokenizers can realize, leaving the OPD loss form itself unchanged. We show that these units are the finest jointly tokenizable supervision interface, and that coarser alternatives remove teacher-student distinctions that are useful for on-policy learning. Across three heterogeneous teacher-student pairs on mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, SimCT shows consistent gains over shared-vocabulary OPD and representative cross-tokenizer baselines, with ablations confirming that the improvements come from recovering supervision discarded by exact shared-token matching. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/sunjie279/SimCT-}{https://github.com/sunjie279/SimCT-}.

title: HIMMEL: Hierarchical Interleaved Multi-stream Motion Encoding for Long Video Understanding
summary: Long video understanding with multimodal language models suffers from three compounding bottlenecks: heavy decode cost to obtain dense RGB frames, token growth with frame count, and weak motion perception under sparse keyframe sampling. Existing remedies either prune visual tokens after decoding, which leaves the expensive RGB pipeline untouched, or they discretise codec motion vectors with a generative tokeniser, which couples motion modelling to a heavy pre-training stage. In this paper we present HIMMEL, a hierarchical video-language framework that allocates semantic and motion capacity along separate paths. A small set of sparse semantic anchor frames is routed to the expensive host ViT to ground object identity and scene layout, while the far denser inter-frame intervals are encoded by a lightweight compressed-domain tri-stream adapter that distils motion evidence from motion-vector maps, residual maps, and an I-frame context branch into aligned motion tokens. These tokens are injected into the LLM via a differentiable placeholder mechanism, after a dedicated Stage 1 contrastive alignment that places the motion representation in a geometry compatible with the frozen visual backbone. We further show that an InfoNCE alignment objective beats MSE regression by +1.5 pp. On Video-MME, HIMMEL surpasses the dense 32-frame baseline by +2.3 pp (61.2 to 63.5%) while using 3.6 times fewer context tokens and running end-to-end in 1.03 s per question instead of 2.75 s. Switching to a stronger Qwen3-VL-8B host pushes HIMMEL to 64.9%, narrowing the gap to much larger proprietary systems while keeping inference on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU. Extensive ablations across stream composition, motion-encoder family, fusion mode, alignment objective, anchor count, LoRA rank, and video duration confirm that the full tri-stream contributes to the observed gains, and that the benefit grows with video length.

title: HAServe: Horizon-Aware Scheduling and Memory Co-Design for Efficient LLM Serving
summary: Online large language model (LLM) services process requests that share context but differ in prefix structure and arrival timing. Finite capacity couples request admission and key-value (KV) retention. This paper addresses one online serving problem: using a unified view of visible demand to choose the feasible joint admission and KV-retention candidate with the lowest predicted latency cost as prefix structures and arrival rates vary. To model this problem, we introduce HorizonSchema, a workload abstraction that connects exact prefix paths, permitted serializations, and released consumers as shared inputs to both decisions. Our analysis shows that useful reuse depends on demand and prefix survival, while service order changes latency even at equal computation. Furthermore, we present HAServe, which turns this abstraction into a scheduling--memory co-design method of systematic optimization for online LLM serving. We implement HAServe on SGLang and evaluate Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Llama2-13B on five workloads using eight H100 GPUs. Across the evaluated workloads, HAServe achieves up to $1.14$--$5.90\times$ P99 TTFT speedups and up to $1.08$--$1.44\times$ the throughput, with KV-cache hit rate up to 20.59 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline for each metric and setting.

title: TabFORGE: A Tabular Foundation Model for Generative Modelling
comments: Accepted by the Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Generative modelling is a demanding test of foundation models, because it requires robust, holistic representation learning for a given data modality, rather than optimisation for a supervised prediction target alone. While recent work on tabular foundation models has achieved remarkable progress in predictive modelling, generative tabular foundation models remain underexplored. Existing tabular foundation generators, in particular, have not yet consistently matched strong dataset-specific generators in synthetic data quality. A key reason is their insufficient alignment with the inter-feature dependency structure of tabular data, which can reflect underlying causal relationships. In this paper, we address this gap by introducing a novel tabular foundation model, $\textbf{TabFORGE}$, built on pretrained $\textbf{Tab}$ular $\textbf{FO}$undational $\textbf{R}$epresentations for $\textbf{GE}$neration. TabFORGE is designed to utilise transferable representations induced by a pretrained structure-aware feature encoder, which captures information useful for characterising inter-feature dependencies. It further decouples latent modelling from decoding through a two-stage design: we first pretrain a score-based diffusion transformer, and then pretrain a denoising-aligned decoder using the denoised latent embeddings. This design elegantly mitigates the distribution shifts in latent embeddings that typically arise between training and inference. We evaluate TabFORGE comprehensively against 22 benchmark methods on 45 real-world datasets. Our results show that TabFORGE effectively learns and leverages generalisable tabular representations, enabling efficient generation of high-quality synthetic tabular data, particularly with strong structural fidelity. Code is available at https://github.com/SilenceX12138/TabFORGE.

title: Recovery Models for Linear Batch Codes
comments: Long version of a paper submitted to ISITA 2026
summary: Various types of recovery algorithms for batch codes have been considered previously, including asynchronous recovery and recovery algorithms arising from Almost Affinely Disjoint (AAD) families. We initiate a systematic investigation of linear batch codes equipped with recovery algorithms. We introduce online and strongly online batch codes, investigate their relations with asynchronous batch codes, and introduce (m,L)-strongly online batch codes, which provide particularly simple recovery algorithms. We then study simple batch codes associated with arbitrary bipartite graphs, obtaining graph-theoretic conditions for such codes and generalizing several known results.
comment: Long version of a paper submitted to ISITA 2026

title: Locking Pretrained Weights via Deep Low-Rank Residual Distillation
summary: The quality of open-weight language models has dramatically improved in recent years. Sharing weights greatly facilitates model adoption by enabling their use across diverse hardware and software platforms. They also allow for more open research and testing, to the extent that users can use them as checkpoints, fine-tune them according to their needs, and potentially redistribute them. In some cases, however, concerns on modifying these weights towards unauthorized uses may outweigh the pros of giving users such freedom. Defending against such adaptation is non-trivial: since an adaptive attacker can observe all weights and architectures by definition, they can reverse simple structural defenses, and use optimization to defeat the simplest locking mechanisms. In this work, we exploit the inference-training asymmetry of automatic differentiation as a novel defense axis. We propose DLR-Lock, a method where the purveyor of the model purposely replaces each pretrained MLP in their model with a deep low-rank residual network (DLR-Net) of comparable parameter count, forcing activation memory that grows linearly with depth during backpropagation. DLR-Nets are efficiently trained via module-wise regression. We show that, beyond this memory overhead, DLR-Lock results in architectural mismatches that complicate the optimization landscape of standard fine-tuning, and a backward pass that incurs disproportionately more overhead than the forward pass. Our defense succeeds in withstanding adaptive attackers with full knowledge of the defense strategy while preserving the original model's capabilities. Experiments on LLMs validate these claims.

title: Conditioning Strengthens Classical Entropy and Matrix Inequalities: A Submodular Approach
summary:
Dembo, Cover, and Thomas (1991) developed an elegant information-theoretic framework for proving determinantal inequalities for positive definite matrices, which relies on the structural inequalities of differential entropy. Submodular functions, which subsume entropy, inherently satisfy these structural inequalities because they obey generalized forms of the fundamental properties of entropy -- a chain rule and the property that conditioning reduces the function's value (under an appropriate definition of conditioning). Applying subadditivity, Han's inequality (1978), and partition subadditivity (i.e., subadditivity over a partition) yields Hadamard's, Szász's, and Fischer's inequalities, respectively. Furthermore, this framework recovers Ky Fan's inequality (1955), a strengthening of Hadamard's inequality. We highlight a previously unnoticed information-theoretic insight behind this improvement: conditioning yields a tighter upper bound on the joint entropy than the unconditional one.
  In this paper, we establish conditional strengthenings of Han's inequality and partition subadditivity in the general setting of submodular functions. We derive equality conditions for these strengthened bounds and characterize when they strictly improve their unconditional counterparts. We specialize these results to differential entropy and apply them to establish strengthened versions of Szász's and Fischer's inequalities. The strengthening of Szász's inequality recovers Ky Fan's inequality as a special case, and is strictly stronger than the classical Szász's inequality for any non-diagonal positive definite matrix. We also derive an inequality concerning eigenvalues, which generalizes and strictly strengthens a corresponding eigenvalue inequality of Ky Fan. We provide numerical examples to explicitly illustrate the tightness of our proposed matrix determinantal bounds.

title: Plan Before You Trade: Inference-Time Optimization for RL Trading Agents
summary: Reinforcement learning agents for portfolio management are typically trained and deployed as static policies, with no mechanism for policy adjustments using price forecasts at inference time. We propose FinPILOT (Financial Plugin Inference-time Learning for Optimal Trading), a plugin inference-time policy optimization framework inspired by Model Predictive Control (MPC). Under the price-taker assumption, portfolio actions do not affect future market prices, allowing a multi-step price forecaster to provide imagined market trajectories without iterative action-conditioned rollouts. At each decision step, FinPILOT uses the forecaster's predicted price trajectory to construct an allocation-based imagined return objective and optimizes the pretrained policy at inference time before executing one step of the trade. Our framework is compatible with any pretrained policy and adapts the policy using the forecaster's predictions without modifying the original RL training pipeline. Evaluated with five pretrained policies (PPO, SAC, A2C, TD3, DDPG) across DJ30 equities and foreign exchange (FX) over three rolling held-out test years (30 settings in total), FinPILOT improves Total Return in 28 of 30 settings and Sharpe ratio in 27 of 30, with gains spanning both stochastic and deterministic policies. Direct single- and multi-period portfolio optimizers supplied with the same forecasts do not reproduce these aggregate gains under our evaluation protocol. Further, using controlled forecasts at calibrated quality levels, we show that both the magnitude and consistency of FinPILOT's performance increase as forecast error is reduced.

title: Neurodata Without Boredom: Benchmarking Agentic AI for Data Reuse
summary: Neuroscience data are fragmented across labs, experimental paradigms, and storage formats, and data reuse often requires substantial manual effort. Standardized formats have been proposed in response, but a fundamental tension persists: formats flexible enough for diverse experiments are rarely self-explanatory, while fully descriptive datasets demand documentation and curation effort that few labs can sustain. Coding agents, which can read code and text quickly with apparent attention to details humans tend to skim, are a natural candidate to reduce this burden. To measure how well coding agents perform data reuse, we benchmark them on eight recent papers with large-scale mouse neural recordings spanning diverse recording modalities, behavioral paradigms, and formats. Given the data, code, and paper, the agents must reformat the data for a common downstream task: training a decoder from neural activity to task and behavioral variables. Evaluating the resulting solutions, however, is challenging, since many conversion decisions are under-specified and several choices are defensible. Yet a subtle but scientifically significant error can invalidate the dataset in ways aggregate metrics can miss. We therefore pair outcome-based metrics with a process-based rubric, scored by two human evaluators against manual reference solutions. We find that agents succeed on most subtasks but rarely produce a fully error-free end-to-end solution; we characterize their mistakes and suggest data-sharing practices for agent-assisted reuse. Finally, we find that agent judges are unreliable at catching errors on their own, but can automate process-based evaluation when given reference solutions.

title: Language-Based Agent Control
summary: This paper introduces language-based agent control (LBAC), a new programming model for agentic applications that brings techniques from programming languages and language-based security to the problem of agent control. In conventional programming, combinations of static typing and runtime enforcement have long been used to guarantee that well-typed programs satisfy user-specified policies, including policies for access control, information flow, data provenance, and more. The key idea behind LBAC is to extend these guarantees to agentic applications by requiring agents to generate programs that are themselves well typed in the context of the surrounding scaffolding code. Unsafe programs are rejected by the type-checker before execution, allowing policies to apply uniformly across the entire application, including both agent-generated behavior and developer-written scaffolding. At the same time, LBAC preserves substantial expressiveness: agents may perform arbitrary side-effect-free computation and recursively invoke subagents, which retain full tool access subject to the same -- or potentially more restrictive -- policies. We demonstrate LBAC with three case studies: I/O sandboxing via filesystem capabilities, data provenance, and information-flow control.

title: PREPING: Zero-Task Agent Memory Construction via Self-Practice
summary: Agent memory is typically constructed either offline from curated demonstrations or online from post-deployment interactions. However, regardless of how it is built, an agent faces a cold-start gap when first introduced to a new environment without any task-specific experience available. In this paper, we study pre-task memory construction: whether an agent can build procedural memory before observing any target-environment tasks, using only self-generated synthetic practice. Yet, synthetic interaction alone is insufficient, as without controlling what to practice and what to store, synthetic tasks become redundant, infeasible, and ultimately uninformative, and memory further degrades quickly due to unfiltered trajectories. To overcome this, we present Preping, a proposer-guided memory construction framework. At its core is proposer memory, a structured control state that shapes future practice. A Proposer generates synthetic tasks conditioned on this state, a Solver executes them, and a Validator determines which trajectories are eligible for memory insertion while also providing feedback to guide future proposals. Experiments on AppWorld, BFCL v3, and MCP-Universe show that Preping substantially improves over a no-memory baseline and achieves performance competitive with strong playbook-based methods built from offline or online experience, with deployment cost $2.99\times$ lower on AppWorld and $2.23\times$ lower on BFCL v3 than online memory construction. Further analyses reveal that the main benefit does not come from synthetic volume alone, but from proposer-side control over feasibility, redundancy, and coverage, combined with selective memory updates.

title: SR-Prominence: A Crowdsourced Protocol and Dataset Suite for Perceptually-Weighted Super-Resolution Artifact Evaluation
comments: accepted to NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets track
summary: Modern image super-resolution methods generate detailed, visually appealing results, but they often introduce visual artifacts: unnatural patterns and texture distortions that degrade perceived quality. These defects vary widely in perceptual impact--some are barely noticeable, while others are highly disturbing--yet existing detection methods treat them equally. We propose artifact prominence as an evaluative target, defined as the fraction of viewers who judge a highlighted region to contain a noticeable artifact. We design a crowdsourced annotation protocol and construct SR-Prominence, a dataset suite containing 3,935 artifact masks from DeSRA, Open Images, Urban100, and a realistic no-ground-truth Urban100-HR setting, annotated with prominence. Re-annotating DeSRA reveals that 48.2% of its in-lab binary artifacts are not noticed by a majority of viewers. Across the suite, we audit SR artifact detectors, image-quality metrics, and SR methods. We find that classical full-reference metrics, especially SSIM and DISTS, provide surprisingly strong localized prominence signals, whereas no-reference IQA methods and specialized artifact detectors often fail to generalize across datasets and reference settings. SR-Prominence is released with an objective scoring protocol that allows new metrics to be benchmarked on our suite without further crowdsourcing. Together, the data and protocols enable SR artifact evaluation to move from binary defect presence toward perceptual impact. SR-Prominence is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/imolodetskikh/sr-artifact-prominence.
